title: One verified example is enough for existence

frames.text: The domain contains exactly 1, 2, and 3. Each row records whether that input has square 4. Only the row for 2 is true.
The outlined row supplies a witness: 2 is in the domain and its square is 4. The other rows may be false without defeating an existential claim.

creation: Original native vector table. The three true-or-false cells are computed from $x^2=4$ at $x=1,2,3$. Labels T and F explicitly show truth without relying on shading.
limitations: This is an exhaustive check of the stated three-element domain only. It makes no claim that 2 is the only integer whose square is 4.

title: A witness in every row is not one witness for all rows

frames.text: Both variables range over $\{1,2\}$, and $R(x,y)$ means $x=y$. A cell is true exactly when its row label equals its column label. Each row has a true cell, so $\forall x\exists y\,R(x,y)$ is true.
With $x=1$, choose $y=1$. The outlined row has one true cell.
With $x=2$, choose $y=2$. The witness may change when the input changes.
Fixing $y=1$ fails at $x=2$: this column is not all true.
Fixing $y=2$ fails at $x=1$. Neither candidate works for both inputs, so $\exists y\forall x\,R(x,y)$ is false.

creation: Original native vector table of equality on the two-element domain $\{1,2\}$. Rows are $x$ choices; columns are $y$ choices. Authored highlights inspect each possible row and column.
limitations: This finite counterexample shows that the two quantifier orders are not generally equivalent. Some other predicates do make both statements true.

title: An element and a subset answer different questions

frames.text: Each large box represents the set named at its top. $B$ contains the numbers 1 and 2. Its element 1 is also the only member of $A$, so $A$ is a subset of $B$.

The small outlined object $\{1\}$ inside $C$ is itself a set. Thus $\{1\}$ is an element of $C$, while it is not an element of $B$. $C$ contains the set $\{1\}$ and the number 2, but not the number 1 as a separate element.

creation: Original native drawing of $A=\{1\}$, $B=\{1,2\}$, and $C=\{\{1\},2\}$. A small outlined box denotes an element that is itself a set; unboxed numbers are numerical elements. The large boxes display separate collections.
limitations: The number labels denote ordinary numerical objects, distinguished from sets containing them. Box size and position carry no membership meaning.

title: Follow the membership condition

frames.text: The rectangle is $U=\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$. $A$ = $\{1, 2, 4\}$ and $B$ = $\{2, 3, 4\}$. The shaded union contains 1, 2, 3, and 4: members of either circle, including their overlap.
The shaded intersection contains 2 and 4. Each lies inside both circles.
$A$ minus $B$ contains only 1: it lies inside $A$ and outside $B$. The common members 2 and 4 are excluded.
The complement of $A$ in $U$ contains 3, 5, and 6. Everything outside $A$ but inside the rectangle is selected.

creation: Original native Venn drawing using exact membership in $U=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, $A=\{1,2,4\}$, and $B=\{2,3,4\}$. Every number is positioned according to its two membership tests; native path union, intersection, and difference select the matching regions.
limitations: Areas do not represent counts. The captions list every selected member, so shading is not the only way to identify the result. This example illustrates the definitions, rather than proving a general identity.

title: Outside the union means outside both sets

frames.text: First locate the union, containing 1, 2, 3, and 4. Its complement must exclude every one of these members.
Outside that union are exactly 5 and 6. They are outside $A$ and outside $B$, so they also form the intersection of the two complements.
Now locate the intersection, containing 2 and 4. Its complement must exclude only these common members.
The remaining members are 1, 3, 5, and 6. Each is outside $A$ or outside $B$ (possibly both), so these also form the union of the two complements.

creation: Original native regions computed from the same six-element universe and the same $A$ and $B$ as the set-operation example. The four states show each operation and then its complement inside the fixed rectangle.
limitations: The drawing verifies this finite example. The element proof in the lesson establishes the general laws. Geometric areas have no numerical significance.

title: The power set contains sets as its elements

frames.text: The large box $A$ contains the two elements $a$ and $b$. The large box $\mathcal P(A)$ contains four elements, each drawn as a small outlined set: $\{\}$, $\{a\}$, $\{b\}$, and $\{a,b\}$. Here $\{\}$ means the empty set.
Each small outlined set is one possible selection from $A$. Include neither element, only $a$, only $b$, or both. These are all four subsets, and each is an element of $\mathcal P(A)$.

creation: Original native nested-set drawing. The elements of $A$ are $a$ and $b$; $\mathcal P(A)$ contains exactly the four subsets obtained by deciding independently whether to include each element. Empty braces inside a small box denote the empty set.
limitations: The large boxes display two different sets. Their physical sizes do not represent cardinalities; count their immediate elements instead.

title: Subtract the extra copy of the overlap

frames.text: $A$ has 3 members and $B$ has 3. Adding $3 + 3$ counts 2 and 4 twice. The two common members form the intersection.
Subtract the intersection size 2 once: $3 + 3 - 2 = 4$. The distinct members of the union are 1, 2, 3, and 4. Members 5 and 6 belong to neither set.

creation: Original finite membership drawing using $A=\{1,2,4\}$ and $B=\{2,3,4\}$. Counts come from the listed objects, not from circle areas.

title: Every element belongs to exactly one block

frames.text: $A$ contains 1, 2, 3, and 4. $B_1$ contains 1 and 3; $B_2$ contains 2 and 4. Every member of $A$ appears in exactly one of these two blocks.
Both blocks are nonempty. They share no element, and together they cover $A$. These are all three requirements for a partition.

creation: Original native drawing of $A=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and the two subsets $B_1=\{1,3\}$, $B_2=\{2,4\}$. Subscripts label the blocks; they do not count their members.

title: The same relation as arrows and matrix entries
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs

frames.text: On $A$ = $\{a,b,c\}$, the relation contains exactly $(a,a)$, $(a,b)$, and $(b,c)$. The loop records $(a,a)$; the two other arrows record the other pairs. No unshown pair belongs.
Use $a,b,c$ in both row and column order. The three 1 entries record exactly the three listed pairs. The 0 entries record absent pairs.
The outlined vertex $a$ has two outgoing arrows: its loop and the arrow to $b$. There is no arrow from $a$ to $c$.
Row $a$ is $1,1,0$. Its entries record those same two outgoing arrows and the missing arrow to $c$.

Highlighting a vertex emphasizes its outgoing edges; the corresponding matrix state outlines that row.
limitations: Positions carry no numerical meaning. An arrow returning to its starting vertex records a pair whose two entries are the same.

title: Locate the exact reason a property fails

frames.text: Every vertex has its loop, so the relation is reflexive. Apart from loops, the only arrows are from 1 to 2 and from 2 to 3.
The arrow from 1 to 2 has no reverse, so symmetry fails. No two distinct vertices relate in both directions, so antisymmetry holds.
Following 1 to 2 and then 2 to 3 demands the direct pair $(1,3)$ for transitivity. That pair is absent, so this is a counterexample to transitivity.
Row 1 is 1,1,0. Its final zero confirms that $(1,3)$ is missing. Replacing that zero with 1 repairs the missing shortcut in this example.

creation: Original native graph and matrix for the exact five pairs $(1,1)$, $(2,2)$, $(3,3)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,3)$. Every diagonal entry is 1, reverse off-diagonal pairs are absent, and the two-step chain $1,2,3$ has no direct pair $(1,3)$.
limitations: The final state describes a repair but still displays the original relation. Finding one failed implication refutes a property; claiming a property holds requires considering every relevant pair or triple.

title: Congruence groups the finite domain into whole classes

frames.text: Restrict the domain to $A$ = $\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}$. The three displayed boxes are its congruence classes modulo 3. Their labels choose 0, 1, and 2 as representatives.
The displayed class $[0]$ contains 0, 3, and 6. Any two have a difference divisible by 3.
The other classes are $\{1,4,7\}$ and $\{2,5\}$. The three classes are disjoint and together contain every element of the specified finite domain.

creation: Original native grouping of the integers 0 through 7 by their remainders on division by 3. Remainders 0, 1, and 2 give the three classes shown.
limitations: These are classes in the restricted finite domain. The corresponding classes on all integers contain infinitely many additional members.

title: Read each cover comparison upward

frames.text: This is the power set of $\{1,2\}$, ordered by inclusion. Each join goes from a subset below to a set covering it above. Arrowheads and loops are omitted by the Hasse convention.
The upward sequence $\varnothing$, $\{1\}$, $\{1,2\}$ recovers the comparison $\varnothing\subseteq\{1,2\}$. There is no direct cover because an intermediate subset exists.
Neither $\{1\}$ nor $\{2\}$ has an upward path to the other. They are incomparable, even though each lies between $\varnothing$ and $\{1,2\}$.

creation: Original native Hasse drawing of all four subsets of $\{1,2\}$. Cover pairs add exactly one element. Stored edges are ordered from the lower subset to the upper subset, although the Hasse display deliberately omits arrowheads.
limitations: This drawing encodes inclusion, not numerical comparison or physical distance. Read paths upward; an arbitrary undirected route does not establish an order comparison.

title: Two triangles make a rectangle

frames.text: For $n=3$, rows of the unmarked triangle contain $1,2,\ldots,3$ squares. The diagonally marked squares form a reversed copy. Together they fill a $3\times4$ rectangle, so one copy has $6$ squares.
For $n=4$, rows of the unmarked triangle contain $1,2,\ldots,4$ squares. The diagonally marked squares form a reversed copy. Together they fill a $4\times5$ rectangle, so one copy has $10$ squares.
For $n=5$, rows of the unmarked triangle contain $1,2,\ldots,5$ squares. The diagonally marked squares form a reversed copy. Together they fill a $5\times6$ rectangle, so one copy has $15$ squares.

title: Different first cuts, the same total

frames.text: Start with a $3\times4$ board of 12 unit squares. Dashed lines mark the unit grid; solid borders delimit the current pieces.
One vertical break makes pieces with 3 and 9 squares. Strong induction gives $3-1$ and $9-1$ further breaks, so the total is $1+2+8=11$.
A different first break makes pieces with 4 and 8 squares. Now the count is $1+(4-1)+(8-1)=11$. The general argument uses arbitrary smaller piece sizes summing to 12.

creation: Original native 4-column, 3-row grid. Authored states partition all 12 cells into rectangular pieces; no cells overlap or disappear. The second and third states are alternative first cuts, not consecutive cuts.
limitations: A break splits one existing piece into two along a grid line. No stacking pieces for a single break is allowed. The finite drawings illustrate the general piece-count proof.

title: A construction has parts and subparts

frames.text: The top dot $R$ is the root, representing the whole construction. Its children are a finished part $L_1$ and a part $S$ that splits further. The outlined bottom dots $L_1,L_2,L_3$ are leaves: parts with no further splitting.
There are 3 leaves and 2 internal nodes. Each internal node has exactly two children, so this is a full binary tree. Its left subtree has one leaf; its right subtree has two.

creation: Original native diagram with connections $\{R,L_1\}$, $\{R,S\}$, $\{S,L_2\}$, and $\{S,L_3\}$. Positions indicate parent above child. Labels are identifiers, not numerical values.
limitations: This is one construction tree, not the proof that every full binary tree has one more leaf than internal nodes. The proof must handle both smaller subtrees.

title: Each leaf is one completed choice

frames.text: Choose one of two starters, $A$ or $B$, then one of two endings, 1 or 2. The four leaf labels $\mathrm{A1}$, $\mathrm{A2}$, $\mathrm{B1}$, $\mathrm{B2}$ are the complete outcomes.
The highlighted route chooses $A$ then 2. Every outcome has one route, and every route ends in one outcome, giving $2\cdot2=4$.

title: An empty run means an empty box
section: Repetition without order: distributing identical objects

frames.text: The code $\star\star\mid\mid\star\star\star$ assigns 2 tokens to box 1, none to box 2, and 3 to box 3. Adjacent bars preserve the empty middle box. There are five stars and two bars.

title: Seven objects cannot fit one per box

frames.text: This allocation puts 7 objects into 3 boxes, with occupancies $2,3,2$. Some box must contain at least $\lceil7/3\rceil=3$: if all had at most 2, their total would be at most 6.

title: A term depends on two predecessors

frames.text: For $a_0=0$, $a_1=1$, and $a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$ for integers $n\geq2$, arrows point from the term being computed to the earlier terms it needs. Thus $a_3$ requires $a_2$ and $a_1$.
The term $a_2$ in turn requires $a_1$ and $a_0$. The initial conditions stop this dependency chain. The shared $a_1$ is one sequence value, even when needed more than once.

title: Count calls and work at each level

frames.text: For input size $n=4$, the root performs 4 units of additional work. Its two children have input size 2 each. Numbers on nodes give input sizes. Subscripts $L$ and $R$ distinguish the left and right calls; $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$ distinguish the four calls of size 1. These letters are labels, not variables or multipliers.
The next level contains two calls, each doing 2 units of additional work. The level total remains $2\cdot2=4$.
The four leaves each cost 1. Total work is $4+4+4=12$, agreeing with $4\log_2 4+4$. Subscripts merely distinguish calls of the same size.

title: The bound begins at a threshold
section: Big O: an eventual upper bound

frames.text: The solid curve is $f(n)=n+3$ and the dashed curve is $2n$. At $n_0=3$ they meet; for every integer $n\geq3$, $n+3\leq2n$. This supplies $c=2$ and $n_0=3$ for $f(n)=O(n)$.

limitations: The cost functions have integer inputs; continuous connecting curves help compare their values. The algebra $n+3\leq2n$ for $n\geq3$ proves the eventual bound, not the finite plot.

title: Different shapes on a shared scale

frames.text: On the same axes, compare $n$ (solid), $n\log_2 n$ (dashed), and $n^2$ (dotted). At $n=8$, their values are 8, 24, and 64. Line patterns and labels distinguish the curves.

title: A circle becomes an ellipse
section: A small example you can verify

frames.text: The dashed unit circle maps to the solid ellipse under the matrix with rows (0,2),(1,0). Its semiaxes have lengths two and one. The arrows identify output directions, not the path traveled by one point. Here u sub one is the output unit vector (1,0), and u sub two is (0,1).

title: Three directions, but a dependent collection

frames.text: The vectors u=(1,0), v=(0,1), and w=(1,1) are pairwise nonparallel, but w=u+v. The dashed diagonal is reachable from the other two, so the three-vector collection is dependent. Independence tests the whole collection, not just pairs.

creation: Original coordinate drawing from the three explicit endpoints. Horizontal and vertical coordinates use identical units. The equality w=u+v is checked component by component: (1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1).
limitations: Only three representative arrows are shown. Their spans include arbitrary real combinations and are not limited to these finite arrow lengths.

title: Two directions that stay on their own lines

frames.text: For A with rows (2,1),(1,2), u=(1,1) becomes Au=(3,3), the dashed longer arrow on the same line. The vector v=(1,-1) stays unchanged. These eigenvalues are three and one: both special directions remain on their original lines even though their scale factors differ.

creation: Original coordinate SVG with input arrows (1,1),(1,-1) and computed output (3,3). Multiplication by rows (2,1),(1,2) independently gives Au=(3,3) and Av=(1,-1). Both axes use equal units.
limitations: The drawing verifies these particular directions for this matrix. It does not claim every input is an eigenvector; for example (2,0) maps to (4,2), off its original line.
